children: The East African region is inching closer to a full rollout of Free Routes Airspace (FRA), with trials scheduled to end in December, unlocking more destinations, shorter flights, and fuel savings for airlines in the region, potentially cutting the cost of flying across the region.
Flights in the region currently have to follow pre-determined fixed airways, which are often longer, costing airlines more in fuel costs, which is partly to blame for the high air fares.
Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania are among six East African nations that have been experimenting with free routes airspace in the region, and are set to fully operationalise it by the start of next year.

The African Airlines Association (Afraa), which has championed the rollout of FRAs across Africa, says carriers in the region stand to benefit significantly from free routes operationisation in East Africa after a success story in the West African airspace.“We are sure they (East African airlines) will be saving a lot in terms of fuel consumption and CO2 emissions, and also operational costs,” said Abderahmane Berthe, Afraa’s secretary-general.

FRAs allow airline to follow shorter flexible airways between two destinations as the weather allows and at their own discretion, rather following a strict path set by regulators and air traffic service (ATS) navigation providers.

According to Afraa, the continent continues to rely on fixed networks of ATS airways build around ground-based navigation several decades ago, and this remains among the key issue limiting competitiveness of African airlines.

Yet, implementing FRAs has remained challenging due to fragmented airspaces, and different navigation service providers from one country to another, or from one region to another. West and Central Africa became the first regions to fully deploy FRAs in October last year after successful trials that began in November 2023. In June, the region’s FRAs went a notch higher by removing pre-approval requirement for carriers’ chosen routes.
However, it was easier to roll-out out in the West and Central African region because they have fewer navigation service providers, with several countries in the two regions sharing providers.
East and Central Africa could be a little more complicated because of a more fragmented airspace, but MR Berthe says trials have proved successful, and full roll-out is expected soon.
He said although there’s certainty these benefits will be felt in East Africa at full roll-out as well, it is still hard to estimate to what extent exactly.

Vincent Owino“It’s not easy to estimate because every airline operates different routes and the saving on fuel depends also on the type of aircraft they are operating,” said Mr Berthe in an interview with The EastAfrican.
For carriers in the region, the initiative comes at a timely moment, amid elevated fuel costs on the continent, which has significantly raised their operating costs and thinned their profit margins.

Kenya Airways, Jambojet, and RwandAir have all seen up to 70 percent jump in fuel their fuel costs in the aftermath of the Iran conflict, with fuel now accounting for at least 30 percent of their operating costs.
Jambojet said it had to reduce its flights to keep the soaring costs at bay, while Kenya Airways also abandoned some routes and reduced frequencies on others.
With the expected fuel savings, airlines in the region could add frequencies on regional routes, as well as cut fares, boosting air connectivity in the bloc.
